The velocity of sound in seawater varies from about 1450 m/s to 1550 m/s, increasing with increases in temperature, salinity, and pressure (depth).
The deep sound channel (SOFAR channel) typically occurs around 1200 m depth in mid-latitudes and can extend over distances of more than 3000 km.

The Thorp equation describes the frequency dependence of the sound absorption coefficient in the ocean, with three terms accounting for low-frequency relaxation, magnesium sulfate ion-pair absorption, and high-frequency water relaxation.

Diffraction effects can dominate the attenuation of very low-frequency sound (below 0.2 kHz) in shallow water, while diffusive scattering from oceanic microstructure can contribute significantly to attenuation above 0.1 kHz.

Laboratory studies have identified that the low-frequency sound absorption in seawater is due to a relaxation process associated with the boric acid-borate equilibrium, with a large increase in volume accompanying the overall process.
The boric acid pKa in seawater ranges from 8.86 at 5°C to 8.61 at 25°C, at a salinity of 36%.
Boron in seawater occurs primarily as inorganic borate species, with only 1-3% of the total boron associated as organically bound boron.

Variations in oceanographic parameters like temperature, salinity, pH, and total boron concentration can affect the relative concentrations of boric acid and borate, influencing the low-frequency sound absorption.
The typical low-frequency sound absorption coefficient in the deep ocean SOFAR channel is on the order of 0.05 dB/km at 500 kHz.

The boric acid-borate equilibrium is coupled with other equilibria in seawater, contributing to the total alkalinity and having the capacity to complex with various metal ions, which likely influence the observed low-frequency acoustic absorption.
Extrapolation of laboratory results on the boric acid-borate system to the ocean environment is complicated by the presence of other competing reactions and equilibria.

The relative contributions of diffraction, scattering, and absorption processes to the overall attenuation of low-frequency sound in the ocean can vary significantly depending on the specific oceanographic conditions.

Accurate interpretation of experimental data on low-frequency sound attenuation in the ocean requires careful consideration of the various physical and chemical factors that can influence the observed results.
The study of low-frequency sound absorption in the ocean is an active area of research, with implications for underwater acoustics, oceanography, and marine chemistry.
The paper highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between physicists, engineers, and chemists in advancing the understanding of sound propagation in the marine environment.
